controversies/filioque-controversy/quest: Does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father alone, or from the Father ‘and the Son’ (Filioque)?
controversies/filioque-controversy/summa: A single Latin word added to the Creed in Spain (589) became, after Photius (867), a central doctrinal point dividing Eastern and Western Christianity. The dispute combines Trinitarian theology (how the persons are distinguished) with ecclesiology (who may change an ecumenical creed).
controversies/filioque-controversy/sides: Western: ‘and the Son’

Everything the Father has he gives to the Son, except being Father. The Spirit is called ‘the Spirit of his Son’, and the risen Christ breathes him on the apostles. If the Son had no part in the Spirit's eternal origin, nothing would distinguish Son from Spirit. We confess, with Augustine, that the Spirit proceeds principally from the Father, and from the Son as the Father's gift — one principle, not two. The phrase was added to defend the Son's equality against Arians, not to change the faith.
Galatians 4:6 and Romans 8:9: the Spirit belongs to the Son.
John 16:14–15: the Spirit receives from what is the Son's, and all that the Father has is the Son's.
Relations of origin are needed to distinguish the persons (Anselm, Aquinas).
Greek fathers (Cyril, Maximus) spoke of procession ‘through the Son’.
No regional church may alter the creed of an ecumenical council.
It undermines the Father's monarchy or blends Father and Son.
John 15:26
John 20:22
Galatians 4:6
Romans 8:9
Eastern: ‘from the Father’ (alone)

Christ himself said the Spirit ‘proceeds from the Father’. The Fathers of 381 confessed exactly that, and the whole Church sealed it. The Father alone is the source of deity; the Son is begotten and the Spirit proceeds, each uniquely from him. To make the Son a second cause either divides the divine monarchy or turns Father and Son into a single impersonal principle. And when one bishop changes the creed of all, the conciliar nature of the Church itself is wounded.
John 15:26 says ‘from the Father’ without qualification.
Ephesus (431) forbade composing a different creed.
Personal properties are not shared: causing belongs to the Father alone.
The Son's sending of the Spirit is temporal (the economy), not eternal origin.
Eternal relations should be revealed by temporal missions.
Without a Son–Spirit relation of origin the persons are not clearly distinguished.
John 15:26
John 14:16
controversies/filioque-controversy/timel: Creed of Constantinople: the Spirit ‘proceeds from the Father’.
Council of Ephesus forbids any other creed (canon 7).
Toledo III adds Filioque in Visigothic Spain.
Council of Aachen under Charlemagne endorses the Filioque; Pope Leo III affirms the doctrine but refuses to add it to the creed, displaying the original text on silver shields.
Photius' encyclical condemns the Filioque as heresy.
Filioque sung at Rome at the coronation of Emperor Henry II (traditional date).
Mutual excommunications; the Filioque among the charges.
Second Council of Lyon defines double procession; union short-lived.
Council of Florence: Laetentur Caeli union; rejected in the East.
Vatican clarification: the Father as sole source; Greek ekporeusis distinguished from Latin processio.
North American Orthodox–Catholic Consultation recommends the Catholic Church use the original creed.
controversies/filioque-controversy/resol: Unresolved but softened. Catholics, Lutherans, Reformed and most Protestants retain the Filioque in liturgical use (Rome omits it in Greek); Eastern and Oriental Orthodox and the Assyrian Church of the East reject it. Agreed statements since 1995 suggest the theological gap is narrower than the historical polemic, while the ecclesiological question (authority to amend the creed) remains.
controversies/filioque-controversy/conse: A lasting doctrinal marker of the East–West schism.
Shaped reunion councils (Lyon 1274, Florence 1439) and their failure.
Stimulated distinctive Orthodox pneumatology (Lossky) and Western reconsideration in the ecumenical age.
controversies/regulative-vs-normative-wo: May the church use in worship whatever Scripture does not forbid, or only what Scripture commands?
Regulative vs normative principle: psalms, hymns, organs and holy days

From the Reformation onwards Protestants divided over how Scripture governs worship. Lutherans and Anglicans kept much of the inherited liturgy; Reformed and Puritan churches removed everything without positive warrant. Later disputes over hymns, organs and a cappella singing grew from the same root.

God has told us how he wishes to be worshipped, and he has judged those who offered "strange fire". Sincerity does not sanctify inventions. Keeping to what Scripture commands guards God’s glory and the believer’s conscience from every human imposition.
Freedom of conscience from human ceremonies
No complete New Testament worship code

Christ commanded the Word and sacraments and left the rest to the church’s freedom, to be ordered "decently and in order". The church may keep its inherited treasures of chant, vestment and calendar, purified by the gospel, and need not tear down what is not contrary to Scripture.
Opens the door to human inventions

If worship must be warranted, then God’s own songbook, the Psalms, is what we should sing, with the voice that God gave us. Inspired songs cannot err; human hymns and instruments add what God did not ask for.
Instruments belong to the Temple cult
Luther’s Formula Missae retains a purified Latin Mass; Zwingli abolishes the Mass in Zurich in 1525.
The first Book of Common Prayer.
Vestiarian controversy: Puritans refuse the surplice.
Directory for Public Worship replaces the Prayer Book.
Prayer Book restored; some 2,000 ministers ejected.
Watts’s Hymns and Spiritual Songs challenges exclusive psalmody.
Churches of Christ and Disciples divide, partly over instruments.
The Free Church of Scotland permits hymns and instruments.

Unresolved and largely denominationally settled: Lutherans and Anglicans follow the normative principle; confessional Presbyterian and Reformed churches profess the regulative principle but apply it in diverse ways; exclusive psalmody survives in small Covenanter and Free Presbyterian bodies; a cappella worship defines the Churches of Christ.
Distinct worship cultures among Protestant families.
Ongoing debates over hymns, bands and seasons in Reformed churches.
controversies/mass-after-vatican-ii/ques: Should the Roman Rite be celebrated in its reformed form only, or also in its pre-conciliar form?
controversies/mass-after-vatican-ii/titl: The Mass after Vatican II: reform, tradition and Traditionis Custodes
controversies/mass-after-vatican-ii/summ: Vatican II mandated reform of the liturgy; the resulting Mass of Paul VI (1969) was embraced by most Catholics but resisted by traditionalists who saw a rupture. Popes have alternately restricted (1970s, 2021) and liberalised (1984, 1988, 2007) the older Mass.
controversies/mass-after-vatican-ii/side: An ecumenical council, guided by the Holy Spirit, asked for the rites to be renewed so that the whole people of God could take part fully and consciously. The reformed Missal is the fruit of that council and of a century of scholarship. Keeping two parallel rites has come to divide the Church and to signal rejection of Vatican II.
Reform went beyond the Council’s text

The Mass our forebears prayed for centuries, which formed saints, cannot suddenly become harmful. Liturgy grows organically; it is not manufactured by committees. The older rite expresses the sacrifice and the sacred with a clarity many Catholics, including young people, find nowhere else, and it should be welcomed, not suppressed.
controversies/mass-after-vatican-ii/time: John XXIII’s final edition of the Tridentine Missal; Vatican II opens.
Missal of Paul VI; Cardinals Ottaviani and Bacci criticise it.
Indult Quattuor abhinc annos permits limited use of the 1962 Missal.
Lefebvre consecrates bishops and is excommunicated; Ecclesia Dei establishes communities using the older rite.
Traditionis Custodes restricts the older Mass.
controversies/mass-after-vatican-ii/reso: Open. The Mass of Paul VI is the ordinary and, since 2021, the "unique" expression of the Roman Rite; celebration of the 1962 Missal continues under episcopal and Vatican restrictions, in the Society of St Pius X (in irregular canonical status) and in Ecclesia Dei communities. Future papal policy remains uncertain.
controversies/mass-after-vatican-ii/cons: Polarisation between liturgical progressives and traditionalists.
Renewed scholarly debate about continuity and rupture in Vatican II.
